sections.title: Introduction
sections.extract: Subject indexing—the process of determining what a work is about, selecting appropriate controlled vocabulary terms, and encoding them as subject access fields in a bibliographic record—remains one of the most time-consuming and cogni- tively demanding components of library cataloging. sections.title: Traditional Machine Learning Approaches
sections.extract: Efforts to automate subject indexing predate the current genera- tion of large language models. National libraries have pursued machine learning solutions for over a decade, typically framing the task as an extreme multi-label text classification (XMTC) problem in which documents must be assigned labels from a vocabulary of tens or hundreds of thousands of controlled terms (D’Souza et al., 2026). sections.title: Present Contribution
sections.extract: The existing literature reveals a consistent pattern: AI systems can identify relevant topics in a document, but they struggle to translate those topics into properly constructed LCSH strings that comply with the Subject Headings Manual. sections.title: Strengths of the Agent Skill Approach
sections.extract: The modular pipeline design offers several advantages over monolithic prompting: Separation of concerns. Each skill addresses one phase of the subject indexing process, mirroring the cognitive stages a trained subject cataloger moves through. sections.title: Comparison Baseline Considerations
sections.extract: The Harvard Library bibliographic dataset serves as a conve- nient but imperfect baseline. Subject headings in a production ILS may reflect varying levels of cataloging (full, core, mini- mal), copy cataloging from diverse sources with differing sub- ject indexing practices, legacy headings predating current SHM instructions, and batch processing or automated enrichment. sections.title: Conclusion
sections.extract: This study demonstrates that a modular agent skill pipeline can produce LCSH subject heading assignments that are conceptu- ally aligned with professional subject indexing practice. The system’s strengths—specificity, named entity identification, and adherence to current LC policy—complement its weaknesses in subdivision completeness and synonym navigation.
